summary: Defines a YANG data model for the Babel routing protocol. It lets network management tools configure Babel and inspect its state in a standard way.

plainLanguage.summary: Babel is a way for network devices to tell each other the best roads for traffic. This gives a standard settings sheet so one tool can manage Babel on many different devices.

subtitle: A standard YANG schema for configuring Babel routers and reading their state.

tldr.problem: Babel routers from different vendors need a common way to be configured and monitored by network management tools.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the ietf-babel YANG 1.1 module, based on the Babel information model, which augments the standard routing module with settings, security credentials, statistics, neighbors and routes.
tldr.outcome: Management systems can use YANG-based protocols such as NETCONF and RESTCONF to manage Babel over IPv6 the same way across implementations.

today: RFC 9647 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2024. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 9647 defines a data model for the Babel routing protocol (RFC 8966). The model is written in YANG 1.1, is compatible with the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA), and is based on the Babel information model in RFC 9046.

The model only includes data nodes that are useful for managing Babel over IPv6. It describes what can be configured and what can be read back, but not how the Babel protocol itself works.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a remote control with the same buttons for every brand of TV. This document designs the buttons for Babel routers.

sections.title: How the Module Fits In
sections.content:
The module augments the YANG routing management module (RFC 8349) so that Babel plugs into a common structure shared by routing protocols, including routes and Routing Information Bases. It also references interfaces defined by the YANG interface management model (RFC 8343), and it adds an identity named babel for the routing protocol type.

There is one caveat about the information model. It mandates some attributes, such as the implementation version and the router ID, and they are read-only. YANG has no way to require that a read-only attribute be present, so the implementation must make sure those mandatory read-only attributes are really there.
sections.plainLanguage: The Babel settings are added to a shared binder that all routing protocols use, so every protocol keeps its notes in the same place.

sections.title: The Tree of Settings and State
sections.content:
Under the babel container sit the version (read-only), an enable flag, the router ID and sequence number (both read-only), and a statistics-enabled flag. Beneath them are subtrees for constants, interfaces, mac-key-set, dtls and routes.

The constants subtree holds the UDP port for Babel messages (default 6696) and the IPv6 multicast group for announcements (default ff02::1:6). The routes subtree is read-only and describes each known route: its prefix, source router ID, the neighbor that advertised it, the received and calculated metrics, the sequence number, the next hop, and flags for whether the route is feasible and whether it is selected.

The enable leaf has two meanings. Written, it configures whether the protocol should be enabled. Read from the operational datastore, it shows whether the protocol is actually running.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings are organized like folders on a computer: one for basics, one for each network connection, one for secret keys, and one for the list of roads the router knows.

sections.title: Interfaces and Link Defaults
sections.content:
Each entry in interfaces points at a network interface and sets whether Babel is enabled on it, the metric-algorithm (two-out-of-three or etx), whether split-horizon is used, and timers such as mcast-hello-interval and update-interval, both in centiseconds. Read-only counters record packets sent and received, with a neighbor table for each interface.

A router can often infer these settings from the interface name. A wired interface such as eth0 is assumed to use two-out-of-three with split horizon on, and a wireless one such as wlan0 is assumed to use etx with split horizon off. A tunnel interface cannot be detected, so its parameters must be configured. Defaults can also be overridden, for example for a wired link feeding a wireless radio, or for a metered 3G fallback link that needs much higher time constants to limit control traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Some roads the router can recognize on its own, like spotting a paved road versus a dirt path. For odd cases, you tell it what kind of road it is.

sections.title: MAC and DTLS Security Subtrees
sections.content:
Two subtrees carry credentials for Babel's security mechanisms. The mac-key-set subtree holds named sets of keys for MAC authentication (RFC 8967). Each key has a value, an algorithm (hmac-sha256 or blake2s), and flags for whether it is used to send and to verify. The dtls subtree holds certificates and private keys for DTLS (RFC 8968), with certificate types x-509 and raw-public-key.

In both, a default-apply flag says whether the set is automatically added to newly created interfaces. Interfaces then select sets through mac-key-sets and dtls-certs, and have flags such as mac-verify, which requires incoming packets to carry a valid MAC.

The module also defines two actions. reset clears statistics for one interface, so a system-wide reset means calling it for every interface. test checks whether a MAC key and algorithm produce an expected MAC for a given input string.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers can lock their messages so only friends can read them. This part holds the keys and certificates, and lets you test a key without showing its secret.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be accessed through NETCONF or RESTCONF, which have mandatory-to-implement secure transports and mutual authentication. Access can be limited with the Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341). The section covers only the data model, not the Babel protocol or its security mechanisms.

Writable nodes are sensitive. The enable parameter can turn Babel off, misconfigured constants can prevent reachability, interface settings can disable security mechanisms, and the key and certificate nodes decide which packets are trusted. Readable nodes can disclose network topology and routes, and credentials, including private ones, are required not to be readable. The test action is designed not to reveal the MAC key, and implementations SHOULD use a constant-time comparison to avoid side-channel leaks.
sections.plainLanguage: The settings can break the network or leak secrets if the wrong person touches them. So only trusted people should be allowed to change or view them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA registered the URI urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-babel in the IETF XML Registry, with the IESG as registrant. It also registered the module in the YANG Module Names registry with the name ietf-babel, the prefix babel and the namespace above, citing RFC 9647. The module's first revision is dated 2024-10-10.

Appendix A of the RFC gives a complete tree diagram and XML configuration examples, including enabling statistics with HMAC-SHA256, letting autodetection set wired and wireless interfaces, and overriding the defaults for a wireless-bridged Ethernet, a tunnel and a metered fallback link.
sections.plainLanguage: The module got an official name tag in the public registry so nobody else uses the same name.
